title: Trauma primary survey (xABCDE)
subject: surgery-trauma
summary: Team-based xABCDE primary survey (ATLS 11th edition): control exsanguinating external bleeding first, then airway with spinal protection, breathing, circulation with blood-based resuscitation and haemorrhage control, disability and exposure, treating each life threat as it is found before the secondary survey.

sections.title: Prepare and activate
items: Activate the trauma team for a high-energy mechanism (fall from height, ejection, pedestrian or rider struck, entrapment), penetrating injury to the head, neck, torso or proximal limb, or abnormal physiology.
Take a structured pre-alert or handover (MIST: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment) and allocate roles before arrival: leader, airway, circulation, procedures, scribe.
Resuscitate while you assess: team members work in parallel, each life threat is treated as it is found, and the patient is reassessed after every intervention.
Older adults, pregnancy, beta-blockers and anticoagulants can mask shock or worsen bleeding; a normal blood pressure does not exclude major haemorrhage.

sections.title: x and A: exsanguination and airway
items: x: control exsanguinating external bleeding before the airway. Firm direct pressure, then a windlass tourniquet high and tight on a limb if pressure fails; pack junctional wounds (groin, axilla, neck) with haemostatic gauze and hold pressure. Record the tourniquet time.

A: check patency (talking, stridor, gurgling, facial or neck trauma, burns). Suction, chin lift or jaw thrust without head tilt, oropharyngeal airway; avoid nasal airways if a basal skull fracture is suspected.
Restrict cervical spine movement with manual in-line stabilisation during airway manoeuvres in any patient with a mechanism for spinal injury.

Definitive airway by drug-assisted rapid sequence induction and intubation if the airway cannot be maintained, GCS is 8 or less, or there is hypoventilation or hypoxaemia. If intubation fails, use a supraglottic device, then front-of-neck access (surgical cricothyroidotomy) if oxygenation fails.

Correct hypovolaemia before or during induction where possible (blood running, reduced induction dose): induction and positive pressure ventilation can precipitate cardiac arrest in the bleeding patient.

sections.title: B and C: breathing and circulation
items: B: expose the chest, count the respiratory rate, look, feel and listen; give oxygen to avoid hypoxaemia, then titrate to avoid hyperoxaemia.

Tension pneumothorax (distress, hypotension, absent breath sounds, distended neck veins): decompress before imaging. Finger thoracostomy in the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line is preferred if skilled, then a chest drain; needle decompression at the same site is a temporising option.
Open pneumothorax: simple occlusive dressing and watch for tension. Massive haemothorax (about 1500 mL on drain insertion): chest drain, blood products and urgent surgical review for thoracotomy.

C: two large-bore IV cannulae (intraosseous if IV access fails); send crossmatch, FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, blood gas with lactate and ionised calcium, and a pregnancy test in women of childbearing age.

Look for the 5 sites of blood loss: external, chest, abdomen, pelvis and retroperitoneum, and long bones. Apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters for suspected pelvic fracture after blunt high-energy trauma.
Bleeding patient: do not use crystalloid in hospital; give red cells and plasma 1:1, activate the major haemorrhage protocol, and give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of injury.
Permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled: target SBP 80 to 90 mmHg (MAP 50 to 60 mmHg) if there is no brain injury; with severe TBI (GCS 8 or less) keep MAP 80 mmHg or more.
Non-responders and transient responders go straight to haemorrhage control (theatre, angioembolisation); do not send an unstable patient to CT.

sections.title: D and E: disability and exposure
items: D: record GCS as separate eye, verbal and motor scores, pupil size and reactivity, lateralising signs and any spinal cord level. Check capillary glucose and treat if below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
Falling GCS or unequal pupils: secure the airway, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, get urgent CT head and neurosurgical advice (see the traumatic brain injury protocol).
E: fully expose, then log roll with spinal precautions to examine the back, perineum and axillae; do not log roll a suspected pelvic fracture before pelvic imaging unless essential.
Prevent hypothermia from arrival: warm room, warmed blankets, warmed fluids and blood via a fluid warmer; aim for core temperature 36 to 37°C.

sections.title: Adjuncts to the primary survey
items: Continuous ECG, SpO2, non-invasive blood pressure, respiratory rate and temperature; end-tidal CO2 after intubation.
eFAST in the bay for pneumothorax, haemothorax, pericardial and free abdominal fluid. A negative FAST does not exclude intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding.
Chest and pelvis X-ray in the bay for unstable patients, limited to what is needed to direct intervention.
Contrast-enhanced whole-body CT (vertex to mid-thigh) for adults with blunt major trauma and suspected multiple injuries once responding to resuscitation or haemodynamically normal.
Repeat haemoglobin, lactate and base deficit: an initial normal haemoglobin can mask early bleeding.
Urinary catheter only after excluding urethral injury (blood at the meatus, perineal haematoma); orogastric rather than nasogastric tube if a basal skull fracture is possible.

sections.title: Secondary and tertiary survey
items: Start the secondary survey only when the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way. Return to x and A whenever the patient deteriorates.
AMPLE history: Allergies, Medications (especially anticoagulants and antiplatelets), Past history and pregnancy, Last meal, Events and environment.
Head-to-toe examination: scalp, face, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, perineum, back and every limb with neurovascular status, plus a full neurological examination.
Give analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, and antibiotics within 1 hour for open fractures; splint fractures.
Complete a tertiary survey within 24 hours to find missed injuries, especially in intubated or distracted patients.

sections.title: Definitive care and transfer
items: Damage control surgery for haemodynamic instability not responding to resuscitation; definitive surgery if haemodynamically normal.
Transfer early to a trauma centre when injuries exceed local capability; do not delay transfer for investigations that will not change immediate management.
Before transfer: secure the airway, drains and lines, continue blood products and warming, and send images, drug and transfusion records with a structured doctor-to-doctor handover.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Managing the airway first while the patient exsanguinates from a limb wound.
Large volumes of crystalloid in the bleeding patient: worsens dilutional coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia.
Sending a haemodynamically unstable patient to CT.
Missing a tension pneumothorax after intubation and positive pressure ventilation.
Being reassured by a normal heart rate or blood pressure in older or beta-blocked patients.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.dose: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours
drugs.notes: Only within 3 hours of injury, as early as possible; do not start later unless hyperfibrinolysis is proven.

drugs.name: Red cells and fresh frozen plasma
drugs.dose: 1 unit plasma to 1 unit red cells, given via a warmer
drugs.notes: Replaces crystalloid in the actively bleeding patient; switch to lab or viscoelastic guided therapy as soon as possible.

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10%
drugs.dose: 10 mL IV (6.8 mmol) slowly via a large or central vein, repeat guided by ionised calcium
drugs.notes: Keep ionised calcium in the normal range (1.1 to 1.3 mmol/L) during transfusion.
